content: Evidence indicates that wearing bicycle helmets can reduce the risk of head injuries among cyclists. However, not all cyclists consistently wear helmets. To address this, some countries and jurisdictions have implemented laws mandating helmet use. These laws remain controversial, as critics argue that such legislation might discourage people from cycling, thereby reducing the associated health benefits. Others suggest that improvements in road safety, rather than helmet laws, may be responsible for observed reductions in head injuries. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of bicycle helmet legislation on helmet use, the incidence of head injuries, and any unintended negative consequences. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and TRANSPORT, covering studies published up to 2010. Additional sources, such as government websites, selected journals, and reference lists of relevant publications, were also examined. The review included studies that assessed changes in head injuries, helmet use, or bicycle use before and after the implementation of helmet legislation. Only studies with a concurrent control group and those evaluating legislation at a country, state, or province-wide level were considered. Two authors independently extracted data and assessed the methodological quality of the studies. Due to the heterogeneity of the data, a meta-analysis was not feasible, and the findings were summarized narratively. Six studies met the inclusion criteria, all of which employed a non-randomized, controlled before-and-after study design. In all cases, the helmet legislation applied exclusively to children. Five studies used adults as a control group, while one study used jurisdictions without helmet laws as controls. Among the included studies, one examined bicycle-related mortality, three investigated changes in head injury rates, and three assessed changes in helmet use. None of the studies reported on changes in overall bicycle use or other unintended consequences of the legislation. Three studies demonstrated statistically significant reductions in mortality or head injury rates following the implementation of helmet laws when compared to controls. One study reported a decline in head injuries that was not statistically significant. Helmet use increased significantly in all three studies that evaluated this outcome. However, no studies provided data on potential declines in bicycle use or other adverse effects of the legislation. In conclusion, bicycle helmet legislation appears to be effective in increasing helmet use and reducing head injury rates in the populations targeted by such laws. However, the number of high-quality studies evaluating these outcomes is limited, and no studies have examined whether helmet laws lead to a decrease in bicycle use.
